title: Interface Capacity and Architectural Replenishment Determine Entanglement-Generation Speed in Quantum Networks
abstract: We show that entanglement-generation speed across a fixed network interface is governed by two distinct resources: the entangling capacity of the interface itself and the ability of the surrounding architecture to replenish it with fresh degrees of freedom. For fermionic Gaussian dynamics, we derive the coefficient-sharp bound $\sum_k|\dotθ_k|\leq\frac12\|K_{AB}\|_*$ on the collective speed of the canonical entanglement angles. Explicit Ising-chain rematching trajectories saturate this bound, thereby certifying exact minimum interaction times under the stated control model. Beyond the Gaussian setting, exhaustive optimization of the complete $N=8$ tree--tree family shows that, at fixed interface capacity, first-layer entanglement, connectedness, and edge budget, the saturation depth is exactly classified by rooted architecture. With higher-resolution $x$-only control, variational entanglement-enhancing-field (VEEF) optimization reaches the numerically resolved fast-$X$ optimum in a two-channel benchmark. Across all 21 symmetry-reduced rooted orbits, a pre-specified two-time VEEF growth diagnostic recovers the complete replenishment partition directly from optimized dynamics. Interface capacity therefore sets how much entangling flux is available, whereas architecture determines whether fresh degrees of freedom can continually replenish the interface and sustain repeated use of that capacity.
summary: This work establishes that the speed at which entanglement can be generated in quantum networks is limited by two independent factors: the fixed entangling capacity of the physical interface and the ability of the internal network architecture to continuously supply fresh quantum resources. By analyzing fermionic Gaussian dynamics and complex graph structures, the authors provide sharp bounds and demonstrate that the architecture dictates the sustainability of entanglement generation over time.
main_problem: The paper determines the fundamental speed limit for generating entanglement in quantum networks when the physical interface is fixed, but the internal routing architecture is dynamical and constrained.
main_result: Entanglement generation speed is governed by two distinct resources: the fixed interface capacity (entangling flux) and the ability of the surrounding architecture to continually replenish fresh degrees of freedom.
method: The authors derive theoretical bounds using fermionic Gaussian dynamics and employ advanced optimization techniques like Variational Entanglement-Enhancing-Field (VEEF) optimization across various network topologies.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum network analyzed using fermionic Gaussian dynamics, often modeled by Ising chains or tree-tree architectures. The dynamics are controlled by local rotations and a fixed cross-cut interaction defining the interface.
key_observables: Canonical entanglement angles ($	heta_k$), bipartite entanglement in ebits ($E_A$), and the entanglement-generation speed ($\sum |\dot{	heta}_k|$).
important_parameters: Interface Capacity ($\Lambda_{\partial}$), Architectural Replenishment efficiency, and the network topology (e.g., open vs. periodic Ising chains).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to perform arbitrarily fast on-site rotations and focuses on the distinction between fixed interface flux and architectural replenishment capability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the saturation mechanism in open Ising chains, showing Majorana-rematching trajectories, and map the minimum saturation depth ($L^*$) required for different network topologies.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the core resource constraints, derives the coefficient-sharp bound for Gaussian dynamics, proves saturation using Ising chains, and then extends the analysis to complex tree-tree architectures using high-resolution VEEF optimization to classify the limiting topological resource.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, resource-theoretic understanding of speed limits in quantum information processing, distinguishing between local coupling strength and global connectivity/routing capability.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

The Majorana-rematching trajectory re- peatedly presents a fresh canonical pair to the single physical interface. After stage s, 2s Majorana dimers cross the cut, corresponding to s maximally entangled fermionic mode pairs. The protocol therefore realizes monotonic canonical-angle growth with unit interface utilization and reaches SA = 4 ln 2 at T = 4t0, saturating Eq. (15).

Thick solid bonds are the two fixed cross-cut Ising couplings, dashed bonds are the variable internal tree couplings, and the red dashed line marks the bipartition. (a) Best VEEF entanglement at the common diagnostic time T = 2t0 for all 21 reduced rooted orbits. The pre-specified threshold Ec = 3.70 leaves the three L∗= 3 boundary orbits O08, O16, and O17 unresolved.
